title: Preventive maintenance and client aftercare
audience: Car detailers who arrange maintenance for vehicles they have detailed, and who give the owner aftercare advice.
learningOutcomes: Set a maintenance interval for each protected surface using the product label and the source guidance.
Explain to the owner the signs that protection is wearing, such as poor water beading or dullness.
Give written aftercare advice that does not promise results the product cannot give.

instruction.heading: Why maintenance matters
instruction.body: A detail that is not maintained starts to slip. The Detailing Hand Book describes preventive maintenance as the stage after the first complete detail, when periodic cleaning and the right treatments keep the appearance. It also gives the practical reasons. Dirt works like sandpaper as people get in and out, and it wears fabric and carpet. Acid rain and bird droppings can damage the finish. Dirt that sits in the wheel wells or under the car holds moisture against the metal, and rust can follow. Maintenance also keeps protection working, because protection is a layer that wears away with washing, weather and sun.

instruction.heading: Intervals for each surface
instruction.body: The source guides give typical intervals, and the product label always overrides them. Wash every one to two weeks. Clean wheels at each wash, and give them a thorough clean and a protective layer every two to three months. Clay about twice a year, or before polishing in heavy-contamination areas. Polish one to two times a year, as needed, during a full detail. Reapply sealant about once a season, or sooner when water stops beading. Reapply carnauba wax every three to eight weeks, depending on use and conditions. Clean trim with a light degreaser every one to three months, and re-dress it every one to two months. Clean and protect the engine bay every three to six months. Coatings last one to three years or more, according to the manufacturer. Give the interior a thorough clean once or twice a year. Record these intervals for each vehicle, tie each one to the product it applies to, and explain them in the owner's language.

instruction.heading: Reading the signs
instruction.body: Protection is wearing when water no longer beads and sheets off the paint, when water pools and looks flat, when the surface looks duller after a wash, or when dirt sticks more easily. Teach the owner a simple check: after a wash, see how the water behaves on the bonnet. The Auto-Detailing guide uses this test. Dull wheels and dressing that slings onto the paint are signs that the wheels or tyres need their own treatment. Explain these signs in the aftercare note, so the owner knows when to book rather than waiting for the appearance to fail.

instruction.heading: Aftercare advice the owner can keep
instruction.body: Write aftercare advice the owner can keep. Include the wash frequency, how to dry (blotting with a clean, dry towel rather than dragging it), where to park if possible, and the signs of wear. Advise against degreasers on protected surfaces unless the protection is to be removed, because the Auto-Detailing guide notes that most degreasers remove sealant or wax. Where the product names a maintenance product, use that product rather than a general cleaner that may strip the layer. Advise the owner to wash microfibre towels without fabric softener. Do not promise a result the product cannot give. A statement that a coating lasts for life is not supportable; a statement that the maker's figure applies under stated conditions is. Keep a copy of the advice in the job file, and make the next maintenance date part of the record, not a sales pressure point.

procedure: Record the protection type and product for each surface, and the date it was applied.
Set a maintenance interval for each surface from its product label and the source guidance.
Show the owner the water-beading check and explain the signs of wear.
Write the aftercare note with the wash method, the parking advice and the do-not list.
Agree the next maintenance date with the owner, and record it.
Keep a copy of the note and the schedule in the job file.

workedExamples.situation: A car parked outdoors under trees shows water that stops beading three weeks after a sealant was applied.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What interval and advice do you give?
workedExamples.reasoning: Explain that protection is wearing early because of the parking and the sap, and that the owner should expect a shorter interval than the seasonal guide. Offer a maintenance wash on the interval the owner chooses, with a beading check. Record the new interval and the reason. Do not blame the product, and do not promise a longer period than the maker's figure.

workedExamples.situation: An owner washes the whole car every week with a degreaser and asks why the wax has gone.
workedExamples.reasoning: Explain that a degreaser removes wax and sealant, as the guide notes, so the protection has been stripped at each wash. Recommend a routine shampoo for regular washing, and reserve the degreaser for the areas that need it. Re-protect after any degreased wash, and record the advice.

equipmentAndPpe: Maintenance schedule template for each vehicle.
PPE: none specific to this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Setting one interval for every surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Set an interval for each surface and tie it to its product.
State the maker's figure and the conditions it applies under.

commonErrors.error: Waiting for the owner to ask.
commonErrors.prevention: Set the next date in the record and in the aftercare note.

commonErrors.error: Recommending a degreaser for routine washing.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a routine shampoo; degrease only as needed, and re-protect afterwards.
Give the note and keep a copy in the job file.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Claims in aftercare and sales material must be accurate and supported, and must not leave out material facts (ACCC: false or misleading claims).
Interval figures in this lesson come from the source guides, not from product labels. The label and SDS govern use.

qualityStandard: Each protected surface has a recorded interval tied to a named product.
The owner receives the signs of wear and the aftercare note in writing.
No durability claim goes beyond the maker's figure.
documentationEvidence: Maintenance schedule for each vehicle, with the product and the date of the last protection.
Aftercare note with the owner's acknowledgement.
summary: Maintenance keeps the appearance and keeps the protection working.
Tie each interval to its product and the label.
Give the owner the signs of wear and a written note they can keep.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which sign suggests a sealant has worn?
options: The paint feels warm to the touch after a short wash
Water beads tightly and sheets off the panel as it should
The tyres are dark, which shows the sealant has worn off
Water no longer beads, and begins to pool and look flat

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer wants a lifetime guarantee on a coating. What is the correct response?
options: Promise it, to close the sale and keep the customer happy with the price
Explain that the figure is the manufacturer's stated life under stated conditions
Say it lasts forever if washed weekly, since weekly washing keeps it working
Refuse to discuss durability, since the customer should not be given any figure at all

knowledgeChecks.question: Which routine wash approach is best for protected paint?
options: Wash in direct midday sun, since the heat helps the shampoo lift dirt quickly
A degreaser on the whole car every week to keep the surface clean
Dry wiping with a dry cloth, since that keeps the protection on the surface
A routine shampoo; degrease only where needed, and re-protect after
